answers.U1-S1: The narrator recalls seeing flamingos for the first time at age six on a walk to a river, a moment of wonder that no later sighting ever equaled.
answers.U1-S2: He was young and timid, still fearful of the open plain and its dangers, and not yet confident enough to venture out on his own.
answers.U1-S3: To show how long and tiring the walk was for a small six-year-old boy, making the journey feel like a real effort.
answers.U1-S4: In a slow, grave, dignified way, as if performing something serious and stately.
answers.U1-S5: Because the open wings revealed a glorious crimson color he hadn't seen before, making the bird seem even more beautiful and wondrous.
answers.U1-S6: That the birds were rare or unfamiliar in their area, making the sighting unusual and special; flamingos weren't normally found in their neighborhood.
answers.U1-S7: Because its tall, graceful white-and-rose body and glorious crimson wings seemed so beautiful and heavenly to him that it felt almost otherworldly.
answers.U1-S8: The first sighting was special because he was six and seeing them for the first time, with a child's fresh wonder; novelty and youth made it unmatched.
answers.U1-S9: It moves forward in time to his many later sightings, contrasting them with the first to emphasize that the childhood experience remained the most delightful.
answers.U1-S10: Fond, nostalgic appreciation; he treasures the memory and still regards that childhood moment of wonder as unsurpassed.
